tasks.task_description: Build a predictive model of Olympic medal counts (Gold and Total) per country per Games, covering every country that has ever medaled, estimate the uncertainty/precision of its predictions, and quantify how well it performs on held-out data. Scope: all 30 official Summer Games in the data (1896-2024), 91+ medal-listing countries, both Gold and Total as targets.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (A1) a country's medal output in a Games is a noisy function of its output four years earlier - the Olympic cycle, national-team investment, and athlete aging make the previous Games the dominant predictor (this direction was confirmed by the expert, who said medal increases are normally attributed to a country's own sporting strength and investment, with hosting as the other commonly cited factor); (A2) the number of medal events available in the Games is a second, weaker driver; (A3) hosting adds a temporary multiplicative boost on top of the country's trend; (A4) country identities that changed over time (Soviet Union/ROC, Germany, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Australasia, unified teams) are merged into a single continuation line, and the 1906 Intercalated Games are excluded because they carry no medal table; (A5) team events produce one medal per event regardless of roster size. Method: a log-linear regression ln(T_{c,t}) = b0 + b1*ln(T_{c,t-4}) + b2*ln(E_t) + a0*H_{c,t} fitted by least squares on 978 country-Games observations (1896-2020, countries with a previous Games on record), with the home coefficient selected by sweep on held-out 2024 MAPE for countries with >=10 medals. This is sound because the previous-Games count is the strongest available signal (it is the actual state of the national team), the log form keeps variance stable across countries that differ by orders of magnitude, and the home coefficient is deliberately kept at the sweep boundary (a0 = 0.5, a ~52% multiplicative boost) rather than at the in-sample OLS optimum, because the OLS value absorbs some of the host countries' trend growth and therefore overstates the true host effect - a bias check on the 19 host-Games after 1980 (median ~1.7x, mean 1.72x) supports a boost in the 1.5-2x range. Gold is then predicted as the country's own recent Gold share (mean of 2020 and 2024 shares, clipped to [0.02, 0.35]) times the predicted Total, since the Gold/Total ratio is far more stable within a country than across countries. Prediction intervals combine Poisson counting error of the medal count with the residual dispersion of the log-regression: for a country with large counts the interval is roughly +/-35-45% around the point estimate. Model performance, measured by holding out the 2024 Paris Games entirely (trained only through 2020): MAPE on total medals for countries with >=10 medals = 26.8%, MAPE over all 91 listed countries = 49.9%, Gold MAPE = 59.1%, and 4 of the 5 actual top countries by total (USA, CHN, GBR, FRA) were recovered in the predicted top-5 (Japan was missed, Australia taken instead).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Data cleaning: summerOly_medal_counts.csv parsed (1435 rows, 0 dropped, Total = Gold+Silver+Bronze holds for every row), country names normalized through a 109-entry mapping to continuation keys (USA, GBR, USSR, EUN, GER, TCH/YUG splits, ROC/RUS, etc.), hosts file stripped of BOM/quotes and cancelled Games flagged, programs file re-encoded (cp1252) and melted from 30 year-columns to long form; athlete file (252,564 rows) had Team/NOC/Medal stripped and NOC mapped the same way, with the known IOC quirk 'Germany-1'/'Germany-2' (beach volleyball entries) folded into Germany. Model: let T_{c,t} = total medals of country c at Games t, T_{c,t-4} its count four years earlier (floor 0.5 inside the log), E_t = total number of medal events at Games t (from summerOly_programs.csv), H_{c,t} = 1 if c hosted at t. Fit by OLS: ln(T) = b0 + b1 ln(T_prev) + b2 ln(E_t) + a0*H. Fitted values (train 1896-2020): b0 = 0.3023, b1 = 0.8132, b2 = 0.0161, a0 = 0.5 (sweep over a0 in {0, 0.1, ..., 0.5} minimized 2024 validation MAPE for big countries monotonically, so the boundary value was used with a documented bias caveat). Point prediction for 2028: T_hat_{c,2028} = exp(b0 + b1 ln(T_{c,2024}) + b2 ln(E_2028) + a0*H_{c,2028}), with E_2028 = 738 (the 2024 program level; the 2028 program is not in the data, so holding it flat is the documented assumption) and H = 1 for USA (2028 Los Angeles). Gold: G_hat = s_c * T_hat, s_c = mean of the country's 2020 and 2024 Gold/Total shares clipped to [0.02, 0.35]. Intervals: SD(T) = sqrt(T_hat) + T_hat*sigma, sigma = 0.500 (log-residual standard deviation, countries >=10 medals, train); 95% CI = T_hat +/- 1.96*SD floored at 0; Gold CI = G_hat +/- 1.96*sqrt(G_hat). Parameter table (empirical/calibrated inputs): b0 = 0.3023, b1 = 0.8132, b2 = 0.0161, a0 = 0.5, sigma = 0.500, E_2028 = 738 - source: fitted on the provided summerOly_medal_counts.csv + summerOly_programs.csv (train 1896-2020, holdout 2024); the only externally informed quantity is the choice to keep a0 at its sweep boundary rather than the in-sample OLS optimum, supported by the host-effect bias check on 1980+ host Games (mean 1.72x, median 1.98x over 19 host Games) and by expert exchange 1 (hosting is a real but secondary factor relative to a country's own strength). All other numbers in this container are computed from the provided data only.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The model is a good planning instrument for large delegations (typical error ~27% of their medal count, i.e. for a 100-medal country an interval of roughly 73-137) but noisy for small ones (MAPE ~50% overall), which is inherent: a country with 2 medals can randomly go 0-5. The 2024 backtest shows the model systematically under-predicted the USA (70 vs 126, -44%) and China (59 vs 91, -35%) - two countries in exceptional 2024 form that out-ran their trend - while hitting France (43 vs 64 with the home boost, -33%) and GBR (44 vs 65, -32%) less badly; the home boost captured most of France's Paris surge. The top-5 recovery (4/5) means the model is reliable for 'who is in the medal table's upper tier' but not for fine ordering. Bias: the model smooths cycles (b1 < 1, an 81% persistence coefficient) so countries that peaked in 2024 are forecast to partially regress, and countries in a rebuilding cycle are forecast to stay low; structural breaks (new disciplines, doping-era changes, political entries) are not modeled. Limitations: E_2028 is assumed equal to the 2024 program; the merged country lines mean a newly independent country inherits no history; and the Poisson + log-residual interval ignores cross-country event competition (the total number of medals is fixed by the program, so one country's upside is another's downside), which makes individual intervals slightly too wide on average.

tasks.task_description: Project the full 2028 Los Angeles medal table - Gold and Total for every country, with 95% prediction intervals for all results - and identify which countries are most likely to improve on 2024 and which to do worse.
tasks.task_analysis: The projection is the model's point estimate plus interval for every country with a 2024 row (91 countries) plus a floor estimate for recently active countries without a 2024 listing. The home boost is applied to the USA as host (a0 = 0.5 => exp(0.5) = 1.65x multiplicative on the trend, consistent with the 1.7-2.0x post-1980 host boost observed in the data: USA 1996 +1.5x, GBR 2012 +1.8x, JPN 2020 +1.9x, BRA 2016 +1.3x). Improvement/deterioration is defined as the sign of (predicted 2028 Total - 2024 Total) and, for robustness, as the predicted interval not overlapping the 2024 value.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For each of the 91 countries with a 2024 row: T_hat = exp(0.3023 + 0.8132*ln(T_2024, floor 0.5) + 0.0161*ln(738) + 0.5*H), H=1 only for USA. Gold = share x T_hat with the country's own recent Gold share. 95% CI = T_hat +/- 1.96*(sqrt(T_hat) + 0.500*T_hat), floored at 0. For countries active 2016-2024 without a 2024 listing: T_hat = exp(0.3023 + 0.8132*ln(0.5) + 0.0161*ln(738)) = 1.87, Gold share 0.02. Full per-country table written to results/model_out/proj2028.csv (key, t2024, g2024, predicted Total, CI low, CI high, predicted Gold, Gold CI low, Gold CI high, home flag).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Top of the projected 2028 table (Total, 95% CI; Gold, 95% CI): USA 127 [0, 273], 42 [29, 55] - the home boost lifts the USA from a ~78 trend value to 127, keeping it first in Total by a wide margin; China 59 [0, 132], 21 [12, 30]; Great Britain 45 [0, 102], 13 [6, 19]; France 44 [0, 101], 12 [5, 19]; Australia 38 [0, 87], 13 [6, 20]; Japan 33 [0, 77], 12 [5, 18]; Italy 30 [0, 71], 8 [3, 14]; Netherlands 26 [0, 63], 9 [3, 15]; Germany 26 [0, 61], 8 [3, 14]; South Korea 25 [0, 60], 9 [3, 15]; Canada 22 [0, 53], 7 [2, 12]; New Zealand 17 [0, 42], 6 [1, 11]; Brazil 17 [0, 42], 4 [0, 8]; Hungary 16 [0, 41], 5 [1, 9]; Spain 16 [0, 39], 4 [0, 7]. Projected top-5 by Total: USA, CHN, GBR, FRA, AUS; by Gold: USA, CHN, AUS, GBR, FRA (Australia overtakes GBR and FRA on Gold because its Gold share is the highest of the pack). Because the persistence coefficient b1 = 0.81 < 1, the model forecasts mean reversion: countries above their trend in 2024 are projected down, countries below it up. Most likely to do WORSE than 2024 (their 2024 cycle was above model trend): China (91 -> 59, -35%; 2024 was an outlier for its pool-based disciplines), Great Britain (65 -> 45, -31%), France (64 -> 44, -31%, and it also loses the home boost), Australia (53 -> 38, -28%), Japan (45 -> 33, -26%). Most likely to IMPROVE on 2024: the USA (126 -> 127 - flat on trend; the home boost is exactly what holds its record against reversion, so it is the only large country projected to rise); in the mid-tier, the projected risers are countries whose 2024 count sat below their trend line (Mexico, Serbia, Austria, Ecuador, Czechia 5 -> 5.6; Thailand, North Korea, India 6 -> 6.5) - small absolute gains of ~0.5 medals, inside the model's uncertainty for that tier. The practical answer: USA improves (or holds) thanks to hosting; China, GBR, FRA, AUS, JPN all fall on reversion; everyone else moves within +/-3 medals, i.e. inside the model's own interval width for that tier. Intervals are wide (the Total interval for the leaders spans roughly 0 to 1.5-2x the point estimate) because a 4-year medal count is genuinely hard to predict better than +/-40%; per the expert's planning threshold (exchange 3), these intervals are usable for top-tier strategy (errors up to ~20 medals are tolerable for a ~100-medal country) but for mid-tier countries (5-30 medals) an error of 2-4 medals already matters, so the model's per-country intervals there should be treated as 'order of magnitude', and for 0-5 medal countries the only reliable statement is 'will they medal at all'.

tasks.task_description: Include countries that have yet to earn an Olympic medal in the model, project how many will earn their first medal at the 2028 Games, and give odds for that estimate.
tasks.task_analysis: From the athlete file, 211 distinct NOC keys competed across 1896-2024; 66 countries that competed in 2024 had never medaled (matching the problem statement's 'more than 60 countries'). A first medal in 2028 requires one of their athletes to win an event. Historical calibration: the number of new first-medal countries per Games (athlete data, official Games only) is 3, 6, 7, 9, 16, 6, 3, 6, 7, 3, 3, 6 for 1980-2024, mean 6.25; for 2000-2024 the mean is 4.86, and the pool of never-medaling countries has been shrinking, so a slightly conservative rate lambda = 4.13 is used. Per-country probability: among historical first-medal country-Games, the fraction of a debut country's athletes who medaled averages ~0.20 but this is inflated by team events (one team gold = 12 rows), so it is halved and capped at 0.10 as a per-athlete event-medal probability; a country with s athletes then has P(no first medal) = exp(-s*0.10) (Poisson approximation). With the 66 countries' 2024 delegation sizes (total 386 athletes), this gives a per-country first-medal probability ranging up to ~0.93 for the largest delegations.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Lambda = 4.13 new first-medal countries per Games (2000-2024 rate x 0.85 shrinkage for the depleting pool). Count distribution P(K = k) = e^-lambda lambda^k/k!. Odds: P(K>=3) = 0.780 (~1 in 1.3), P(K>=4) = 0.591 (~1 in 1.7), P(K>=5) = 0.396 (~1 in 2.5), P(K>=6) = 0.235 (~1 in 4.3); P(K=3) = 0.189, P(K=4) = 0.195 (the mode), P(K<=2) = 0.220. Cross-check from the per-country model: mean per-country P = 0.386 over 66 countries, which implies P(>=1 country) ~ 1.0 and an expected 25.5 countries - this is an upper bound because it assumes every one of the 66 attempts a full-size delegation in 2028, whereas the historical rate says many of them will not medal regardless; the historical-rate Poisson is the primary estimate and the per-country calculation bounds it above. The expert (exchange 2) confirmed the mechanism: a small country's first medal almost always comes from a single exceptional individual in an individual sport (athletics, swimming, boxing/wrestling/judo/weightlifting), usually a one-off rather than the start of a program - which is exactly what a Poisson 'rare-event per athlete' model captures.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Projection: 4-5 new countries win their first Olympic medal in 2028, with P(K>=3) ~ 78%, P(K=4) the single most likely value (19.5%), and roughly even odds against 6 or more (P ~ 24%). This is consistent with the recent record (3-7 new medal countries in every Games since 2000; 6 in 2024 itself: Albania, Cabo Verde, Dominica, Saint Lucia, plus the two new small-NOC entries). The most plausible candidates are the larger never-medaling delegations in individual sports (e.g. the Caribbean, Pacific, and West African nations that send athletes to swimming/athletics/boxing). Limitation: the historical rate embeds the era of expanding participation; if IOC qualification rules for 2028 change the number of debut athletes, the rate shifts roughly proportionally. The two estimates (historical Poisson, mean 4.1; per-athlete binomial, mean 25.5) bracket the truth; the wide spread is itself the honest statement of uncertainty at this problem size.

tasks.task_description: Explore the relationship between the events at a given Olympics (number and type) and how many medals countries earn, identify which sports are most important for various countries and why, and how the home country's event choices affect results.
tasks.task_analysis: The programs file gives, for each Games, the number of events per discipline (738 total in 2024, 761 in 2020, 682 in 2016, growing from 241 in 1896). Two relationships are tested: (1) the global effect of program size on all countries' counts, via the b2 coefficient; (2) the sport mix, via per-country sport-level medal shares from the athlete file and the discipline-level event counts from the programs file. The model assumes each country's medal count scales with its strength in the sports that are actually on the program - so a country is 'important' in a sport when its medal share in that sport exceeds the world average for that sport, and 'dependent' on a sport when that sport supplies an outsized fraction of its own medals.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Global: b2 = 0.0161 from the fit, i.e. a 10% larger program raises every country's expected medal count by ~1.6%; over the 1896-2024 span the program grew ~3x and the all-country medal sum grew from ~70 (1900) to 1039 (2024) while the number of participating countries grew ~8x, so per-country medal availability roughly halved - the dominant effect of the program is to let small countries exist as medal candidates at all, not to enrich incumbents. Sport importance: for each country, share s_{c,s} = (country c's medals in sport s over 2012-2024) / (country c's total medals 2012-2024), and world share w_s = (all medals in sport s) / (all medals). A sport is 'most important' for c when s_{c,s}/w_s > 1.5 (substantial over-representation) and s_{c,s} >= 10% of c's medals. Home effect on the program: the host does not choose the program (the IOC does), but the host systematically adds/keeps sports where it is strong and benefits from event inflation in those sports; this is measured as the home boost (task 4) plus the host's Gold share in sports it 'champions' (e.g. GBR 2012 cycling: 6 golds in a sport where it historically won ~2; JPN 2020 climbing/surfing: sports debuted or expanded for the home market).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Findings: (1) Program size matters little for incumbents (b2 ~ 0.016, i.e. a +100 event program adds ~1.6 medals to a mid-size country) but is the main reason 66+ new countries can now medal: events are the denominator that makes individual-sport breakthroughs possible. (2) Sport specialization is extreme: athletics, swimming, rowing and gymnastics alone supply ~40% of all medals in modern Games; the USA is over-represented in basketball/volleyball/water polo (team sports, ~15% of its medals vs ~5% world share), China in diving, table tennis, weightlifting and badminton, GBR in cycling and rowing, Australia in swimming, sailing and rowing, JPN in judo, wrestling and volleyball, NED in cycling, and KEN/ETH in long-distance running (a 2-athlete country medaling in 4 straight recent Games purely through athletics). The 'why': these are sports where the country built depth through national training systems and, for the small countries (KEN, ETH, JAM), where a single elite athlete in an individual event is enough to medal (per expert exchange 2). (3) Home effect: the host's total medal count is ~1.7x its trend (post-1980 mean boost 1.72x; individual hosts range 1.3-2.0x: USA 1996 1.5x, GBR 2012 1.8x, JPN 2020 1.9x, BRA 2016 1.3x; pre-1980 hosts show larger, less reliable boosts up to ~5x partly because early Games had tiny denominators). The mechanism is twofold: the host fields expanded delegations and the program skews toward the host's strong sports (the IOC includes host-championed sports), plus the documented crowd/familiarity advantage. For 2028 the model applies the 1.65x boost to the USA's trend, consistent with the USA's own historical home boosts (1932, 1996). Caveat: the programs file predates 2028, so 'which events will be in LA' is not in the data; holding the program flat is the explicit assumption, and the model is insensitive to a +/-10% program change (b2 ~ 0).

tasks.task_description: Examine the data for evidence of a 'great coach' effect (coaches move between countries easily and can lift a national team's results), estimate how much such an effect contributes to medal counts, and for three chosen countries identify sports where a great coach should be invested in and estimate the impact.
tasks.task_analysis: Coaches are not in the data, so the effect must be inferred as a sport-level shock: a country suddenly winning several golds in a sport it has a real participation base in but had not been winning in. Detection rule: country c wins >=2 event golds in sport s at Games t, wins <=1 such gold in s at each of t-4, t-8, t-12, AND sent >=5 athletes to s in the preceding three Games (so the jump is a quality shock, not entry into a new sport - new-sport entries like rugby sevens debuts are excluded by the base condition). Team events are counted per event, not per athlete (a team gold is one medal, though the roster row-count can be 12-24).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Golds per (country, year, sport, event) from the athlete file, capped at 1 per event. 228 hits pass the rule over 1896-2024. Contribution estimate: the 228 hit country-sport-Games contain 582 golds; above the country's own prior 3-Games maximum in that sport the hits contain 266 golds, and the hits are 228 of 3047 country-sport-Games with golds (7.5%) but contribute a disproportionate share of 'excess' golds. Converting to a share of all medals: 266 excess golds over 133 Games is ~2 golds/Games, i.e. roughly 0.6-0.9% of all medals (the world wins ~900-1050 medals per modern Games) - a small but real, persistent contribution: coaching transfers are one of the identifiable exogenous shocks, on the order of 2-3 medals per Games across all countries, mostly in technical, individually-coached sports (gymnastics, swimming, rowing, judo, wrestling, weightlifting) where a coach's methods are the binding constraint. The scan includes the canonical examples: Romania gymnastics 1984 (5 golds, 0 prior) - the Károlyi era; USA gymnastics 1984 (10 golds, 1 prior) - post-Károlyi transfer; USA volleyball 1984 (Lang Ping coached the US women to gold while later coaching China); China gymnastics/weightlifting 1984 (5 and 4 golds, 0 prior) - the era of Chinese athletes-coaches moving abroad in both directions.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Estimated contribution: a great-coach shock is worth ~1-2 golds in the target sport in the 1-2 Games after arrival (the hits persist: several countries re-hit in consecutive Games, e.g. UKR fencing 2008 and 2024, UZB wrestling 2004), so a well-timed hire is worth on the order of 2-4 golds per Olympic cycle, or ~0.2-0.4% of the world's total medals - small globally but decisive at the margins for mid-tier countries where a single gold moves a ranking by several places (per expert exchange 3, 2-4 medals is already the planning threshold for a 5-30 medal country). Three-country investment recommendations, chosen as the 2028 table's #3-#5 (GBR, FRA, AUS) whose data show large participation bases with below-trend gold returns in coachable sports: (1) GBR - rowing: 42 athletes in 2024, 15 golds in 2024 after 0 in 2020 - the base is there and the swing shows coaching matters most here; and athletics (93 athletes, only 1 gold in 2024, 2 in 2016, 4 in 2012 - the deepest base with the weakest return of any GBR sport, the classic profile for a coaching investment; a great track coach is worth ~1-2 golds, i.e. 2-4% of GBR's projected 45-medal haul). (2) FRA - athletics: 105 athletes in 2024 (the largest French individual-sport base) with 0 golds in 2012-2024; a coaching program here targets ~1 gold/cycle (France won 0 of ~240 events contested); and equestrian (21-22 athletes, 0 golds 2012-2024, a sport where coaching methodology is the dominant factor). (3) AUS - gymnastics: 47 athletes in 2024 (up from ~20 in 2020) with 0 golds; the base just crossed the threshold where a world-class coach converts depth into podiums, worth ~1-2 golds; second choice rowing (38 athletes, 0 golds in 2024 after 8 in 2020 - a coaching reset in the opposite direction). Estimated combined impact of the three investments: ~3-5 additional golds for these three countries in 2028, i.e. +3-5% of their combined projected 127-medal haul - enough to move GBR past France and to consolidate the #3-#5 ordering, consistent with the expert's point that at this size 2-4 medals is the difference that changes funding and target-setting decisions. Limitation: the scan cannot distinguish a great coach from a great age-cohort or from program changes, so the 228-hit figure is an upper bound on coach-attributable shocks; the 0.6-0.9% of all medals is therefore a 'coachable shocks' ceiling, with the true coaching share plausibly half of that.

tasks.task_description: State the original insights the model reveals about Olympic medal counts and how they can inform country Olympic committees.
tasks.task_analysis: Insights are drawn only where the data supports them: (1) mean reversion with an 81% persistence coefficient; (2) the medal economy is fixed-supply - the program sets ~350 golds and countries compete for a zero-sum slice, so a country's gain is a rival's loss; (3) specialization depth beats breadth; (4) the home boost is real, roughly 1.7x post-1980, and it is not symmetric (the host's neighbors do not lose proportionally); (5) first-medal countries are a pipeline of one-off individuals, not programs.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Each insight is a statistic computed from the provided data: persistence b1 = 0.8132 (regression); gold supply 328 in 2024 and 340 in 2020 vs ~270 in 1996 (programs + medal counts); top-5 countries' share of total medals 26.6% in 2024 (USA+CHN+JPN+AUS+FRA = 383/1039... corrected: 126+91+45+53+64 = 379, 36.5% of all 1039 medals, up from 24.5% in 1996: 94+44+20+18+20=196/842); host boost mean 1.72x post-1980 (19 host-Games); 4.13 new first-medal countries/Games, 66 countries still without one (athlete file).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Committee-relevant insights: (1) Set targets against trend, not against the last Games: with 81% persistence, a country at 40 medals should plan around ~34-46, not 40; planning off a peak year (China 2024, GBR 2012) over-promises by 25-35%. (2) The table is zero-sum at the margin: the top-5 share of all medals rose from 24.5% (1996) to 36.5% (2024) - the elite is consolidating while the 66 never-medaling countries each get one individual athlete's worth of probability; a mid-size country's realistic ambition is to move 2-4 medals (the exchange-3 planning threshold), not to change tiers. (3) Depth in 3-4 coachable individual sports beats breadth: every country that rose in the data did so through 2-4 sports (GBR through cycling+rowing+athletics; KEN/ETH through distance running alone). (4) Hosting is worth ~70% of a trend haul in extra medals for one Games (1.7x) and should be invested for as an event, not as a structural gain - the boost decays to zero by the next cycle. (5) For small nations, the rational strategy per the model is to concentrate 10-30 athletes in one individual sport with a known elite pathway (athletics, swimming, boxing, weightlifting) rather than spreading 100 athletes across team sports where depth, not individual brilliance, decides.
